newsitem.title: UK: British manufacturing shows tentative signs of life.
newsitem.headline: British manufacturing shows tentative signs of life.

text.p: British industrial and manufacturing output rose in July, suggesting Britain's beleaguered manufacturers can look forward to the rest of the year with a little more optimism.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed Friday that total industrial production and manufacturing output both rose 0.5 percent in July. That left industrial production 0.9 percent higher year-on-year and manufacturing 0.3 percent better off.
The Treasury welcomed the figures and economists said the pick up in manufacturing, albeit moderate, should herald the start of better things to come.
"Manufacturing prospects for the second half of 1996 are good," Treasury Economics Secretary Angela Knight said.
Most economists agreed. "These figures suggest that manufacturing activity is beginning to turn the corner," said Andrew Cates, an economist at UBS.
Manufacturing has spent the past year firmly in the doldrums. Evidence of buoyant consumer spending has mounted week by week and Britain's service and sales sectors have responded accordingly.
But beleaguered manufacturers, blighted by stockpiles of unsold goods produced in better times last year and weak export markets, have waited a long time for higher spending levels to trickle down.
In June, for instance, manufacturing output fell 0.1 percent, leaving it 0.5 percent below its year-ago level.
But with signs that inventory levels are slowly being unwound and green shoots of recovery beginning to show in continental European markets, the future looks brighter.
"Manufacturers are finally emerging from beneath their stockpiles of unsold goods, assisted by a strong pick-up in consumer spending," Cates said.
Other economists agreed but said substantial improvement for the manufacturing sector might be delayed until next year.

"These are the first signs of an upturn in manufacturing but there is clearly still a long way to go," said Ian Shepherdson, an economist at HSBC Markets. "The real pick-up in output is a story for next year, not this."
The Office for National Statistics said the trend in manufacturing remained broadly flat, as it has been for about 10 months.

But Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident, said a sharp fall in output from the refining industries masked signs of strength in other sectors, most notably in transport equipment, textiles, leather and clothing.
Whether a solid recovery in manufacturing is imminent or may yet be delayed a while, Friday's figures made it even less likely that base interest rates, now at 5.75 percent, will be cut again.

"I think rates have bottomed," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International. "The economy is going to accelerate pretty well from now on in and we will see GDP on a quarterly basis above rather than below trend."
